These days, far fewer people write letters. Email and messages are enough, and above all they are fast. Even so, I still send handwritten letters a few times a year.
It started with a letter from my grandmother when I was a student. The writing was a little shaky, but each character was written carefully. As I read it, I could almost see her sitting at her desk.
Something I could write in a few minutes by email can take over an hour as a letter. But precisely because of that time, I can think slowly about the other person.

The writer is describing how it felt while reading: it was as if she could see her grandmother.
The long time is the reason the writer can think about the other person: からこそ = precisely because.
The next sentence starts with ただ and suggests letters only for special times, so the writer does not intend to use letters for everything.

listening.question: {男|おとこ}の{人|ひと}はどの{教室|きょうしつ}に{参加|さんか}しますか。
options: 「{早|はや}わざお{弁当|べんとう}」
listening.en: On TV, F: From next month the city culture center starts four cooking classes. First, 'Japanese cooking for beginners', which starts from how to use a knife, perfect for people who have never cooked. Second, 'Breads of the world', baking bread from many countries. Third, 'Healthy soups', gentle soups with lots of vegetables. Fourth, 'Quick bento', side dishes for a lunch box you can make in 15 minutes in the morning. Husband: Sounds interesting. I can't cook at all, so I want to learn from the basics. Wife: Bread sounds nice, but making two lunch boxes every morning takes me ages. I want to be quicker, so I'll take this one. Husband: Then I'll take the basic one.
listening.why: He can't cook at all and wants the basics, which is the beginners' Japanese class.
